title: He who is (ST I.13.11)
hook: the best name for God is he who is, being itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, analogy: our words for God are true, and too small. Your line was like, and more. Which ordinary word did you catch pointing past itself? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

A shepherd stands barefoot on a mountainside in front of a bush that burns and is not burned up. A voice has just told him to go back to Egypt and bring his people out. Moses has a practical worry. When I tell them the God of their fathers sent me, he says, they'll ask me his name. What do I say? It's a fair question. And the answer he gets is a strange one: a name that's barely a name at all. Thomas Aquinas comes back to it when he asks which name for God fits best. Today's word is that name.
screen: `A BUSH THAT ISN'T BURNED UP.` → `WHAT IS HIS NAME?` → `A NAME THAT'S BARELY A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here is God's answer to Moses, in the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM." And then: "Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." Thomas asks whether this, He who is, is the most fitting name for God. He says yes, and gives his reasons. The first is what the name means. Every other name we've met names a kind of thing, or a quality. Rock. Shepherd. Wise. Good. This one names no kind at all. It names to be. And remember two days ago: in God, Thomas said, what God is and that God is are one. So a name that means simply is fits God as no other name does. The second reason is how open it is. Other names narrow God down to one side. This one sets no edge. Thomas quotes an earlier teacher, John Damascene, who says this name holds being itself like a sea without limit or bound. Yesterday a girl tried to describe the sea to a friend: you can't see the other side. That's the picture. The third reason is the tense. Not he who was. Not he who will be. He who is. Thomas, following Augustine, says there is no past or future in God. The name is always now. And Thomas, careful as ever, adds a turn. In another respect, he says, the name God, and the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible, are more proper still, because they name God alone. No single name holds God; each catches something. That's analogy, carried all the way. But for this one, being itself, Thomas keeps a special place: the name that points not at something God has, but at what God is.
screen: `I AM WHO AM.` · `NOT A KIND OF THING: TO BE.` · `A SEA WITHOUT LIMIT.` · `ALWAYS NOW, NEVER WAS.` · then, large: `HE WHO IS, HATH SENT ME TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say God is. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say two words slowly, under your breath: God is. Don't add anything. Not God is good, not God is with me. Just God is, and let the words go quiet. Say them again on the next breath out. If you don't pray, try the smallest word of all: is. The floor is. The breath is. The room is. Either way, notice that you're not describing anything. You're only standing in front of being, the way Moses stood in front of the bush. The bell holds the time.
He who is. The name God gives Moses in Exodus, which Thomas Aquinas calls the most fitting name for God: not a kind of thing, but being itself, always now. Today's word.
Your line: being itself. Today, once, stop in the middle of something ordinary and notice simply that it is, before you notice what it is. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic theology, following Thomas, often speaks of God as being itself, and Catholics hear the name from the burning bush in the readings at Mass when Exodus 3 is read.

notes: ST I.13.11 paraphrased: sed contra Exodus 3:13–14; body: the name is most proper because of its signification (existence itself, since God's essence is his existence), its universality (it determines no mode of being; Thomas quotes John Damascene: 'an infinite and indeterminate sea of substance'), and its consignification (present existence; Thomas cites Augustine on no past or future in God). Reply 1: the name 'God' is more proper as to what it is imposed to signify, and the Tetragrammaton more proper still to signify God's incommunicable substance. Confirm.
The Tetragrammaton is referred to as 'the holy name written in the Hebrew Bible' without discussing Jewish practice around it; confirm the wording is respectful and accurate.
Douay-Rheims Exodus 3:14: confirm exact wording ('I AM WHO AM' ... 'HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you').
